claim: Cell-generated forces play a major role in coordinating the large-scale behavior of cell assemblies during development, wound healing, and cancer.
source: Cell-generated forces play a major role in coordinating the large-scale behavior of cell assemblies, in particular during development, wound healing, and cancer.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established scientific understanding about the role of cell-generated forces in biological processes.

claim: Mechanical signals propagate faster than biochemical signals.
source: Mechanical signals propagate faster than biochemical signals, but can have similar effects, especially in epithelial tissues with strong cell–cell adhesion.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact in the abstract without specific experimental data or citation in this sentence.

claim: Mechanical signals can have similar effects to biochemical signals, especially in epithelial tissues with strong cell–cell adhesion.
source: Mechanical signals propagate faster than biochemical signals, but can have similar effects, especially in epithelial tissues with strong cell–cell adhesion.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: After optogenetically activating RhoA in the sender cell, the receiver cell shows an active response so that the cell doublet forms a coherent unit.
source: After optogenetically activating RhoA, a major regulator of cell contractility, in the sender cell, we measure the mechanical response of the receiver cell by traction force and monolayer stress microscopies. In general, we find that the receiver cells show an active response so that the cell doublet forms a coherent unit.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements using traction force and monolayer stress microscopies after optogenetic activation.

claim: Force propagation and response of the receiver cell depend on the mechano-structural polarization in the cell assembly.
source: However, force propagation and response of the receiver cell also strongly depend on the mechano-structural polarization in the cell assembly, which is controlled by cell–matrix adhesion to the adhesive micropattern.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: The response of the receiver cell is stronger when the mechano-structural polarization axis is oriented perpendicular to the direction of force propagation.
source: We find that the response of the receiver cell is stronger when the mechano-structural polarization axis is oriented perpendicular to the direction of force propagation, reminiscent of the Poisson effect in passive materials.
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from the study.

claim: The same effects observed in cell doublets are at work in small tissues.
source: We finally show that the same effects are at work in small tissues.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from experiments on small tissues.

claim: Cellular organization and active mechanical response of a tissue are key to maintain signal strength.
source: Our work demonstrates that cellular organization and active mechanical response of a tissue are key to maintain signal strength and lead to the emergence of elasticity, which means that signals are not dissipated like in a viscous system, but can propagate over large distances.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Active mechanical response leads to the emergence of elasticity, allowing signals to propagate over large distances rather than being dissipated.
source: Our work demonstrates that cellular organization and active mechanical response of a tissue are key to maintain signal strength and lead to the emergence of elasticity, which means that signals are not dissipated like in a viscous system, but can propagate over large distances.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations and modeling.

claim: Cell-generated forces allow cells to probe the mechanical and geometrical properties of their environment.
source: In addition to driving cell shape change and movement, force-producing processes allow cells to probe the mechanical and geometrical properties of their environment (Discher et al., 2005; Luciano et al., 2021), feeding back on to major cellular processes, such as differentiation (Engler et al., 2006; McBeath et al., 2004; Wen et al., 2014; Kilian et al., 2010), fate (Chen et al., 1997; Théry et al., 2005; Nelson et al., 2005), or migration (Pathak and Kumar, 2012; Sunyer and Trepat, 2020; Shellard and Mayor, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Force-producing processes feed back on major cellular processes such as differentiation, fate, and migration.
source: In addition to driving cell shape change and movement, force-producing processes allow cells to probe the mechanical and geometrical properties of their environment (Discher et al., 2005; Luciano et al., 2021), feeding back on to major cellular processes, such as differentiation (Engler et al., 2006; McBeath et al., 2004; Wen et al., 2014; Kilian et al., 2010), fate (Chen et al., 1997; Théry et al., 2005; Nelson et al., 2005), or migration (Pathak and Kumar, 2012; Sunyer and Trepat, 2020; Shellard and Mayor, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Generation of contractile force is a universal property of mammalian cells due to the ubiquitous expression of non-muscle myosin II.
source: Generation of contractile force is a universal property of mammalian cells due to the ubiquitous expression of non-muscle myosin II (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Fast and long-ranged propagation of mechanical force seems to be essential during development when morphogenesis has to be coordinated across the embryo.
source: Fast and long-ranged propagation of mechanical force seems to be essential during development, when morphogenesis has to be coordinated across the embryo (Ho et al., 2019; Desprat et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The onset of migration of neural crest cells in Xenopus appears controlled by the stiffening of the underlying mesoderm resulting from axis elongation.
source: For example, the onset of migration of neural crest cells in Xenopus appears controlled by the stiffening of the underlying mesoderm resulting from axis elongation (Barriga et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The transition from growth to homeostasis in the epithelium of the juvenile esophagus in mice is mediated by the mechanotransduction of progressively increasing mechanical strain at the organ level.
source: An example of a more mature tissue is the epithelium of the juvenile esophagus in mice, whose transition from growth to homeostasis is mediated by the mechanotransduction of progressively increasing mechanical strain at the organ level (McGinn et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Mechanical waves propagate along lengths several orders of magnitude larger than the cell size in confined epithelial tissues.
source: In addition to electrical currents, mechanical waves have also been observed to propagate along lengths several orders of magnitude larger than the cell size in confined epithelial tissues (Di Talia and Vergassola, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Mechanical waves require active cellular behaviors such as contractility and F-actin polymerization to propagate.
source: These waves require active cellular behaviors such as contractility and F-actin polymerization to propagate, suggesting that cells actively respond to external forces to maintain the strength of the signal as it propagates through the tissue (Serra-Picamal et al., 2012; Peyret et al., 2019; Petrolli et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Passive cells in an epithelial tissue act as obstacle for mechanical wave propagation.
source: Furthermore, it has been shown that passive cells in an epithelial tissue act as obstacle for mechanical wave propagation (Ng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In the hydra ectoderm, stress fibers within the cells form a nematic system.
source: Indeed, in some tissues, such as the hydra ectoderm, stress fibers within the cells of the ectoderm form a nematic system (Maroudas-Sacks et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: When plated on H-shaped micropatterns, singlets formed prominent stress fibers around the cell contour (peripheral stress fibers), as well as some smaller internal stress fibers.
source: We found that when plated on H-shaped micropatterns, singlets formed prominent stress fibers around the cell contour (peripheral stress fibers), as well as some smaller internal stress fibers which resulted from the spreading process (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Vertical stress fibers at the edge of the patterns, along the vertical bars of the H, were straight and strongly coupled to the substrate (adherent stress fibers).
source: Vertical stress fibers at the edge of the patterns, along the vertical bars of the H, were straight and strongly coupled to the substrate (adherent stress fibers), while peripheral stress fibers located above the non-adhesive regions of the micropattern, in between the vertical bars of the H, were curved due to the inward pull of the cell cortex (free stress fibers).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Peripheral stress fibers located above the non-adhesive regions of the micropattern were curved due to the inward pull of the cell cortex (free stress fibers).
source: Vertical stress fibers at the edge of the patterns, along the vertical bars of the H, were straight and strongly coupled to the substrate (adherent stress fibers), while peripheral stress fibers located above the non-adhesive regions of the micropattern, in between the vertical bars of the H, were curved due to the inward pull of the cell cortex (free stress fibers).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data with an inference about the cause of curvature.

claim: Focal adhesions were primarily located in the corners of the pattern, although some were present on the middle bar of the H-pattern.
source: Focal adhesions were primarily located in the corners of the pattern, although some were present on the middle bar of the H-pattern, which is required for the cells to spread over the whole pattern.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: A similar pattern of organization was observed in doublets, with the addition of a prominent cell–cell junction in the center of the H-pattern.
source: A similar pattern of organization was observed in doublets, with the addition of a prominent cell–cell junction in the center of the H-pattern, parallel to the lateral bars of the H (Figure 1B), consistent with previous work (Tseng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1B, supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The magnitude of traction forces is very similar between doublets and singlets.
source: By quantifying cell-generated forces using traction force microscopy (TFM), we found that the magnitude of traction forces is very similar between doublets and singlets (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TFM measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The strain energy stored in the substrate is slightly higher for singlets than for doublets, despite spreading over the same surface area.
source: When we quantified the overall contractility by calculating the strain energy stored in the substrate, we found that it is even slightly higher for singlets than for doublets, despite spreading over the same surface area (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by strain energy calculations shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Singlets have to spread a smaller volume over the same surface as doublets, leading to higher tension.
source: This is likely because singlets have to spread a smaller volume over the same surface as doublets, leading to higher tension, both in the actomyosin machinery (Hippler et al., 2020) and in the cell membrane (Pontes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference to explain the observation, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Doublets were unpolarized (average degree of polarization of 0), whereas singlets were horizontally polarized with an average degree of polarization of almost 0.5.
source: Doublets were unpolarized (average degree of polarization of 0), whereas singlets were horizontally polarized with an average degree of polarization of almost 0.5.
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of the stress distribution data.

claim: There is a strong correlation between mechanical and structural polarization.
source: We found the same trend and a strong correlation between mechanical and structural polarization, meaning that the stress fibers in singlets are largely organized horizontally, whereas in doublets they are directed more toward the center (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Intercellular junctions may act as a barrier preventing the horizontal organization of stress fibers that exist in singlets.
source: Our results suggest that intercellular junctions may act as a barrier preventing the horizontal organization of stress fibers that exist in singlets, thus strongly altering the mechanical polarization of the system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The curvature of a free stress fiber results from a balance between an isotropic surface tension pulling the stress fibers toward the cell center and a line tension acting along the fibers.
source: We previously showed that the curvature of a free stress fiber results from a balance between an isotropic surface tension pulling the stress fibers toward the cell center and a line tension acting along the fibers, tending to straighten them (Bischofs et al., 2008; Bischofs et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The radius of curvature is given by the ratio of the line to the surface tension.
source: The radius of curvature is then given by the ratio of the line to the surface tension.
evidence: This is a theoretical relationship from the contour model.

claim: Stress fibers in singlets are subjected to a larger stress along the x-direction than in doublets.
source: The combination of contour analysis and TFM showed that stress fibers in singlets are subjected to a larger stress along the x-direction than in doublets and conversely that stress fibers in doublets are subjected to higher stresses in the y-direction than singlets (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by combined contour analysis and TFM data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Stress fibers in doublets are subjected to higher stresses in the y-direction than singlets.
source: The combination of contour analysis and TFM showed that stress fibers in singlets are subjected to a larger stress along the x-direction than in doublets and conversely that stress fibers in doublets are subjected to higher stresses in the y-direction than singlets (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by combined contour analysis and TFM data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Singlets possessed a significantly larger line tension in their free stress fibers than doublets.
source: Consistent with this, singlets possessed a significantly larger line tension in their free stress fibers than doublets.
evidence: This claim is supported by contour model analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The force exerted by adherent stress fibers was higher in doublets than in singlets.
source: In contrast, the force exerted by adherent stress fibers displayed the opposite behavior: it was higher in doublets than in singlets (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by force measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The presence of cell–cell junction leads to a redistribution of tension from the free to adherent peripheral stress fibers.
source: We conclude that the presence of cell–cell junction leads to a redistribution of tension from the free to adherent peripheral stress fibers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on stress fiber tensions.

claim: In doublets, traction forces increased both in the activated and the nonactivated region after optogenetic activation.
source: In doublets, traction forces increased both in the activated and the nonactivated region.
evidence: This is an observation from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: In singlets, traction forces increased slightly and very locally in the activated region, but decreased in the nonactivated region after optogenetic activation.
source: In the singlets, on the other hand, traction forces increased slightly and very locally in the activated region, but decreased in the nonactivated region (Figure 3C and D, Animations 4 and 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Doublets can establish stable contraction patterns under half-activation of contractility, in contrast to singlets.
source: We conclude that in contrast to singlets, doublets can establish stable contraction patterns under half-activation of contractility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic experiments comparing doublets and singlets.

claim: In doublets, LifeAct fluorescence increases slightly inside and decreases slightly outside of the doublet after photoactivation.
source: In doublets, LifeAct fluorescence increases slightly inside and decreases slightly outside of the doublet.
evidence: This is an observation from LifeAct imaging experiments.

claim: In singlets, LifeAct fluorescence redistributed from the unstimulated side to the stimulated side after photoactivation.
source: In contrast, in singlets, LifeAct fluorescence redistributed from the unstimulated side to the stimulated side, both inside of the cell as well as on the periphery (Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from LifeAct imaging experiments shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The behavior of the nonactivated region in doublets cannot be reproduced with a purely passive reaction.
source: Comparison of the FE results to the experimental data shows that the behavior of the nonactivated region cannot be reproduced with a purely passive reaction (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and B).
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing FEM simulations with experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and B.

claim: Coupling in doublets was positive, meaning that the right half contracts in response to the contraction of the left half.
source: Again, doublets differed from singlets. Coupling in doublets was positive, meaning that the right half contracts in response to the contraction of the left half; whereas it was negative in singlets, meaning that the right half relaxes in response to the contraction of the left half.
evidence: This is a finding from the FEM modeling analysis.

claim: Coupling in singlets was negative, meaning that the right half relaxes in response to the contraction of the left half.
source: Again, doublets differed from singlets. Coupling in doublets was positive, meaning that the right half contracts in response to the contraction of the left half; whereas it was negative in singlets, meaning that the right half relaxes in response to the contraction of the left half.
evidence: This is a finding from the FEM modeling analysis.

claim: Cells in the doublet are actively coupled, with the unstimulated cell responding to the contraction of the stimulated cell by actively contracting.
source: Together, these data indicate that cells in the doublet are actively coupled, with the unstimulated cell responding to the contraction of the stimulated cell by actively contracting, in agreement with previous qualitative reports (Liu et al., 2010; Hino et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Traction force generated by doublets shows a homeostatic response to transient increase of RhoA activity.
source: Strikingly, traction force generated by doublets shows a homeostatic response to this transient increase of RhoA activity. Indeed, once activation is stopped, the traction force generated on the pattern returns to its initial level.
evidence: This is an observation from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: In singlets, transient and local RhoA activation has a destabilizing effect.
source: In singlets on the other hand, transient and local RhoA activation has a destabilizing effect.
evidence: This is an observation from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: The traction stress in singlets keeps decreasing even after the activation is stopped.
source: Furthermore, rather than displaying a homeostatic behavior, the traction stress keeps decreasing even after the activation is stopped.
evidence: This is an observation from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: The cytoskeleton possesses active coupling and the degree of coupling depends on the presence of an intercellular junction.
source: Overall, our data show that the cytoskeleton possesses active coupling and that the degree of coupling depends on the presence of an intercellular junction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing doublets and singlets.

claim: The intercellular junction allows efficient propagation of stress across the whole micropattern, probably due to mechanotransductory pathways and by impeding fluidization.
source: The intercellular junction allows efficient propagation of stress across the whole micropattern, probably due to mechanotransductory pathways and by impeding fluidization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with speculation about the mechanisms.

claim: Active coupling in doublets showed different behaviors in the x- and y-directions, with positive coupling in the y-direction (0.2) and negative coupling in the x-direction (–0.05).
source: Interestingly, this analysis showed different coupling behaviors in the x- and y-directions. We found positive active coupling in the y-direction (0.2), but negative coupling in the x-direction (–0.05) (yellow square, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the FEM model fitting to experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: All forces in y-direction are balanced between the cell and the substrate, but not across the junction.
source: This may be because all forces in y-direction are balanced between the cell and the substrate, but not across the junction.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the observed coupling behavior.

claim: The forces in the x-direction must always be balanced by interaction between the cells across the junction, similar to a 'tug of war'.
source: In contrast, the forces in the x-direction must always be balanced by interaction between the cells across the junction, similar to a 'tug of war.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the observed coupling behavior.

claim: The degree of coupling from contour strain analysis was 0.8, indicating a global active contraction of the unstimulated cell.
source: We found a degree of coupling of 0.8, indicating a global active contraction of the unstimulated cell (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the contour model fitting to experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Active coupling was weaker in TFM measurements than in cortical tension measurements.
source: In conclusion, traction forces, as measured by TFM, show weaker active coupling between activated and nonactivated region than cortical tensions, as inferred by measurement of contour strain.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing TFM and contour strain analyses.

claim: Traction forces are dominated by the activity of the stress fibers, both internal and on the periphery.
source: The traction forces are dominated by the activity of the stress fibers, both internal and on the periphery, because most forces are found in the corners of the doublet.
evidence: This is an inference from the spatial distribution of traction forces.

claim: The contour of the free fiber is determined by the activity of the actin cortex and the free stress fiber.
source: The contour of the free fiber, on the other hand, is determined by the activity of the actin cortex and the free stress fiber.
evidence: This is an inference from the contour model.

claim: Structural and mechanical polarization are tightly correlated and vary greatly between the three different aspect ratios.
source: We found that structural and mechanical polarization are tightly correlated and vary greatly in between the three different aspect ratios (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from experiments with different aspect ratio micropatterns shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: On micropatterns with 1 to 2 aspect ratio, both stress fibers and force patterns were oriented horizontally.
source: For example, on micropatterns with 1 to 2 aspect ratio, both stress fibers and force patterns were oriented horizontally whereas on 2 to 1 they were oriented vertically.
evidence: This is an observation from experiments with different aspect ratio micropatterns.

claim: On micropatterns with 2 to 1 aspect ratio, both stress fibers and force patterns were oriented vertically.
source: For example, on micropatterns with 1 to 2 aspect ratio, both stress fibers and force patterns were oriented horizontally whereas on 2 to 1 they were oriented vertically.
evidence: This is an observation from experiments with different aspect ratio micropatterns.

claim: In 1 to 2 doublets, where cells are polarized mechanically and structurally along the direction of stress transmission, the right cell reacts by relaxing after activation of the left cell.
source: In 1 to 2 doublets, cells are polarized mechanically and structurally along the direction of stress transmission and, after activation of left hand cell, the right cell reacts by relaxing.
evidence: This is an observation from optogenetic experiments with 1 to 2 aspect ratio doublets.

claim: In 2 to 1 doublets, where cells are polarized mechanically and structurally perpendicular to the direction of stress transmission, activation of the left-hand cell leads to contraction of the right-hand cell.
source: In contrast, in 2 to 1 doublets, cells are polarized mechanically and structurally perpendicular to the direction of stress transmission and activation of the left-hand cell leads to contraction of the right-hand cell.
evidence: This is an observation from optogenetic experiments with 2 to 1 aspect ratio doublets.

claim: The degree of active coupling increased with increasing mechanical and structural polarization.
source: We then computed the degree of active coupling as previously and found that the degree of active coupling increased with increasing mechanical and structural polarization (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing optogenetic experiments with different aspect ratios shown in Figure 5D–G.

claim: Mechanical stresses transmit most efficiently perpendicularly to the axis of mechanical and structural polarization in doublets.
source: Altogether, we conclude that mechanical stresses transmit most efficiently perpendicularly to the axis of mechanical and structural polarization in doublets (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experiments with different aspect ratios shown in Figure 5G.

claim: In small monolayers on rectangular micropatterns with aspect ratios of 1:4, the tissue is mechanically and structurally polarized along the long axis of the pattern.
source: We again performed TFM and MSM experiments as well as live imaging of F-actin and quantified the mechanical and structural polarization for micropatterns with aspect ratios of 1:4. We observed prominent actin cables at the periphery of the small monolayers with less marked stress fibers internally. In these conditions, the tissue is mechanically and structurally polarized along the long axis of the pattern (Figure 6A–C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from experiments with small monolayers shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: In small monolayers, an increase in traction forces and cell stress was observed both in the activated and in the nonactivated region after photoactivation.
source: In our experiments, we observed again an increase in traction forces and cell stress both in the activated and in the nonactivated region.
evidence: This is an observation from optogenetic experiments with small monolayers.

claim: In small monolayers, active coupling is higher when the direction of stress propagation is perpendicular to the axis of mechanical and structural polarization of the tissue.
source: We computed the degree of active coupling in the same way as for doublets using our FEM model and found that active coupling is higher, when the direction of stress propagation is perpendicular to the axis of mechanical and structural polarization of the tissue.
evidence: This is a finding from FEM model analysis of optogenetic experiments with small monolayers.

claim: The correlation between mechano-structural polarization and active coupling observed in doublets is also present in larger groups of cells.
source: We conclude the correlation between mechano-structural polarization and active coupling observed in doublets is also present in larger groups of cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing doublet and small monolayer experiments.

claim: Active coupling and its correlation with mechanical and structural polarization seem to be typical for epithelia, independent of size.
source: In summary, active coupling and its correlation with mechanical and structural polarization seem to be typical for epithelia, independent of size (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a conclusion from experiments across different system sizes shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Intercellular forces play a major role in regulating and coordinating tissue morphogenesis.
source: Intercellular forces play a major role in regulating and coordinating tissue morphogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Discussion.

claim: Mechanical forces participate in long-range signaling, propagating over large distances at which they can be received and interpreted by other cells.
source: Recent work has shown that mechanical forces participate in long-range signaling, propagating over large distances at which they can be received and interpreted by other cells (Vishwakarma et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Force signal propagation within cellular assemblies is an active process whose amplification mechanism is controlled by the mechano-structural polarization of the system.
source: By combining quantitative measurements of cellular stresses and cell shape with optogenetic control of contractility and mathematical modeling, here we showed that force signal propagation within cellular assemblies is an active process whose amplification mechanism is controlled by the mechano-structural polarization of the system.
evidence: This is a main conclusion from the study based on experimental data and modeling.

claim: Active coupling between cells was demonstrated before by Liu et al., 2010, but a thorough quantification of this active coupling has been lacking.
source: Our results revealed the presence of active coupling between cells. This was demonstrated before by Liu et al., 2010, but a thorough quantification of this active coupling has been lacking.
evidence: This acknowledges previous work and identifies a gap that the current study addresses.

claim: The active coupling mechanism increases the spatial range a mechanical signal can travel to about one or two cell lengths.
source: This active coupling mechanism increases the spatial range a mechanical signal can travel to about one or two cell lengths according to our data.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: With temporal resolution of one frame per minute, no delay between receiver and sender cell was apparent.
source: Additionally, we tested only transient signals. Maintaining signal strength over longer periods of time could also lead to farther transmission of force signals. Compared to chemical signals, these mechanical signals can travel very fast: indeed, with our temporal resolution of one frame per minute, no delay between receiver and sender cell was apparent.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: In the absence of an intercellular junction, localized contraction leads to actin flow instead of the stress buildup observed in doublets.
source: In contrast, when we carried out the same activation protocol on a single cell that had the same area as the doublets, the nonactivated region displayed acute fluidization of the actin structure. Thus, in the absence of an intercellular junction, localized contraction leads to actin flow instead of the stress buildup observed in doublets.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing optogenetic experiments in doublets and singlets.

claim: Cellularization of the tissue may allow compartmentalization of stress and efficient transmission of stress, allowing the tissue to act as an elastic material rather than a viscous fluid.
source: Therefore, cellularization of the tissue may allow compartmentalization of stress and efficient transmission of stress, allowing the tissue to act as an elastic material rather than a viscous fluid.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations with speculation about the implications.

claim: The magnitude of contraction of the receiving cells relative to the sender cells depends on the direction and magnitude of its mechano-structural polarization.
source: Indeed, our experiments revealed that intercellular coupling strongly depends on the anisotropy of F-actin organization and force distribution. We found that the magnitude of contraction of the receiving cells relative to the sender cells depends on the direction and magnitude of its mechano-structural polarization.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experiments with different aspect ratios.

claim: If the tissue's or doublet's polarization axis is perpendicular to the axis between sender and receiver cells, the receiver cells react more strongly and the signal travels farther.
source: If the tissue's or doublet's polarization axis is perpendicular to the axis between sender and receiver cells, the receiver cells react more strongly and the signal travels farther.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experiments with different aspect ratios and tissue orientations.

claim: The supracellular organization of actin is a major regulator of force propagation within tissues.
source: Finally, our study of epithelial monolayers shows that the supracellular organization of actin is a major regulator of force propagation within tissues.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experiments with small monolayers.

claim: Forces are transmitted more efficiently in a direction perpendicular to the axis of actin polarity also in small monolayers.
source: Forces are transmitted more efficiently in a direction perpendicular to the axis of actin polarity also in small monolayers.
evidence: This is a finding from experiments with small monolayers.

claim: Groups of cells can behave as a 'supracellular unit,' which share many of the characteristics of the individual cells that it consists of.
source: First, recent studies have proposed that groups of cells can behave as a 'supracellular unit,' which share many of the characteristics of the individual cells that it consists of (Vedula et al., 2013; Khalilgharibi et al., 2019; Shellard et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The correlation between mechano-structural polarization and force signal transmission distance holds true across scales.
source: Our findings complement those results, as we show that the correlation between mechano-structural polarization and force signal transmission distance holds true across scales.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing experiments at different scales.

claim: In Xenopus mesoderm during convergent extension, cells are planary polarized in a direction perpendicular to the extension of the tissue.
source: In these tissues, cells are planary polarized in a direction perpendicular to the extension of the tissue, and the convergence and extension of the tissue are driven by directed contraction and migration of the cells (Wallingford et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Preferential transmission of active contraction perpendicular to the polarization axis of the cells could amplify the convergent extension mechanism and contribute to the robustness of the process.
source: Our results suggest that preferential transmission of active contraction perpendicular to the polarization axis of the cells could amplify this mechanism and contribute to the robustness of the process.
evidence: This is a speculation about the implications of the findings for developmental processes.

claim: Opto-MDCK and opto-MDCK LifeAct cells were cultured at 37°C and in 5% CO2 atmosphere in DMEM medium containing 10% heat-inactivated FBS and 1% penicillin/streptomycin.
source: Both cell lines were cultured at 37°C and in 5% CO2 atmosphere in DMEM (Life Technologies) medium containing 10% heat-inactivated FBS (Life Technologies) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Sigma-Aldrich).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Between 20,000 and 50,000 cells were plated on the micropatterned hydrogels.
source: Between 20,000 and 50,000 cells were plated on the micropatterned hydrogels.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Cells were let spread on patterns for 16–28 hr.
source: Cells were let spread on patterns for 16–28 hr.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: On average most doublets seen on the sample at 16-28 hours have started as single cells and divided on the pattern to form a doublet.
source: Data from timelapse experiments (not shown here) showed that on average most doublets seen on the sample at this point have started as single cells and divided on the pattern to form a doublet.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from timelapse experiments.

claim: Cells were checked for mycoplasm contamination and tested negative.
source: Cells were checked for mycoplasm contamination and tested negative.
evidence: This is a statement about quality control of the cell cultures.
